title: Linear Regression
hook: Predict a number by fitting a straight line through your data - the simplest model in ML and the mental blueprint for almost everything that came after.
key_points: A weighted sum of input features predicts the output; learning means finding the best weights.
Training minimizes squared error - penalizing big mistakes more than small ones.
The result is interpretable: each weight tells you how much one feature moves the prediction.
It assumes a linear relationship; nonlinear patterns need richer models built on this same foundation.
content_html: Linear regression is the idea of drawing the best straight line (or flat surface, in more dimensions) through a cloud of data points so you can predict a continuous number - like a house price or tomorrow's temperature - from a set of input features.
extra_html:
How it works

The model multiplies each feature by a learned weight and adds them up, plus a bias term. Training adjusts those weights to minimize the sum of squared differences between predictions and true values - a process called least squares. Because the math is clean, you can often solve it directly rather than relying on gradient descent.

Why it matters

Linear regression is the foundation nearly every ML practitioner builds on first. Its simplicity makes it easy to debug and explain, and the intuition - a weighted sum of features - carries directly into logistic regression, neural networks, and beyond. The Wikipedia article is a good place to dig into the geometry and the math.

related.title: Logistic Regression
related.hook: Take linear regression, squash its output through a sigmoid, and you get a probability - turning a number-predictor into a classifier with one extra step.
